memo:
After a thorough review of the three strategic alternatives for Plant 6, we have selected the "close" option. Closing the plant eliminates a persistent $9.0 million annual loss and, by relocating the product family to higher‑margin plants, lifts Company operating income by $16.5 million per year. The one‑time closure cost of $10 million is modest compared with the recurring $16.5 million earnings uplift, delivering a clear, long‑term accretion to shareholder value over the next twenty years.

Employee impact is handled within the limits set by the board. We will offer relocation to other plants to the maximum feasible 29 employees (15 % acceptance rate), covering $20,000 relocation assistance per person. The remaining 161 positions will be eliminated with a severance payment of $4,566 per employee. This allocation respects the 29‑person cap for moves and stays well within the overall liquidity of $444.9 million.

The closure also preserves $24.3 million of corporate cost allocation, further protecting earnings. No additional capital is required beyond the $10 million shutdown expense, and the company retains the full revenue stream of the product family, now produced more efficiently at existing facilities. This decision aligns with the board’s objective to maximize shareholder value over the long horizon.

We have selected the "close" option for Plant 6 because it delivers the greatest long‑term value to shareholders. Closing the plant eliminates the $9.0 million annual loss and, after reallocating the product family to the remaining facilities, lifts operating income by $16.5 million per year. The one‑time closure cost of $10 million and the severance payments for the 161 eliminated employees (≈$0.74 million) are modest compared with the recurring earnings boost, and the $0.58 million relocation expense for the 29 workers we can move to other plants is fully justified by preserving skilled labor. By moving the maximum 29 employees, we respect the 29‑person limit and retain valuable experience, while the remaining 161 positions are eliminated with a modest severance outlay. The cash impact is a net outflow of roughly $11.3 million today, well within the $444.9 million liquidity cushion, and the ongoing operating margin improvement more than offsets this expense over the next twenty years. This decision also frees capacity at the larger plants, allowing them to absorb the additional revenue ($361 million) without significant incremental cost, further enhancing shareholder returns.

We recommend closing Plant 6 and relocating its product family to the remaining plants.  Closing requires a one‑time $10 million re‑tooling of other sites and eliminates the plant’s $9 million operating loss, raising Company operating income by $16.5 million annually.  After tax, this adds roughly $13 million per year, or about $260 million over a 20‑year horizon, far outweighing the modest one‑time costs of severance ($4,566 per eliminated employee) and relocation ($20,000 per employee who moves).  We will move the maximum 29 employees who accept offers to other plants – the only line open under the “close” option – and eliminate the remaining 161 positions, paying the required severance.  This approach preserves the product family’s revenue, leverages existing capacity (the other plants have $361 million of revenue headroom), and avoids the $30 million capital outlay and limited operating gain of a re‑tool.  The sale option would cut operating income by $15.3 million per year, destroying shareholder value.  Closing Plant 6 therefore maximizes long‑term value creation for shareholders while staying within the Company’s liquidity and workforce limits.
